title: Creator Platforms: Set Clear Scope for Custom Requests Before Accepting Payment
description: A practical workflow for defining custom-request limits, deliverables, payment checkpoints, revisions, timing, and records before accepting paid work through a creator platform.
excerpt: Custom requests can create unclear expectations when a payment, message, and promised deliverable do not line up. Use this workflow to define scope, boundaries, deadlines, and evidence before work begins.
keyTakeaways: Describe the deliverable and its limits in writing before accepting payment.
Check the platform’s current rules for paid requests, messages, and any restricted transaction types.
Agree on timing, revision limits, and what happens if either side cannot proceed.
Keep the request, agreement, payment record, and delivery confirmation together.
Avoid promising work that depends on unclear platform features or another person’s consent.

sections.heading: Treat a custom request as a small project
paragraphs: A paid request is easier to manage when both sides can identify what was agreed. A short written scope can state the kind of deliverable, its format, approximate length or level of detail, delivery channel, and any exclusions. The goal is not to create a complicated contract for every interaction. It is to prevent a payment from being mistaken for an open-ended promise.

Before taking payment, separate the request from ordinary membership access. Confirm whether the buyer expects a one-time item, an ongoing benefit, or access to something already included in a tier. If the distinction is hard to explain in a message, it may also be hard to fulfill consistently. Pause and clarify rather than relying on assumptions.
bullets: Write down the requested deliverable in plain language.
State what is outside the request’s scope.
Confirm which platform feature or permitted payment path applies.
Do not begin until the other person can confirm the same scope.

sections.heading: Check platform rules before offering a transaction
paragraphs: Platform policies can govern what kinds of paid interactions are allowed, where they may be arranged, and how payments or access must be handled. Read the current terms and relevant creator guidance before advertising a custom-request option. A feature that looks convenient is not proof that every use of it is permitted. Rules may also distinguish between public promotion, private messages, subscriptions, and one-time transactions.

Record the policy page or help guidance you consulted and the date you reviewed it. This is a working note, not a guarantee that rules will remain unchanged. If a request appears to fall into a restricted or unclear area, do not try to route it through a different label or an off-platform payment as a workaround. Seek clarification from the platform or decline the request.
bullets: Confirm the permitted transaction route and the platform’s rules for it.
Check any restrictions on promotion, messages, deliverables, or fulfillment.
Keep a dated note of the relevant policy guidance.
Treat unclear or conflicting rules as a reason to stop and clarify.

sections.heading: Define boundaries, revisions, and timing
paragraphs: A scope note should explain how many rounds of reasonable changes are included, what counts as a new request, and when the buyer should expect an update. Do not promise a precise completion time if your schedule is uncertain. A delivery window, with a brief note about when you will communicate if circumstances change, may be more realistic than an unsupported exact deadline.

Boundaries should be specific enough to use. For example, state that requests outside the agreed topic, format, or limits are not included and require a separate discussion, if the platform permits that. Do not imply that payment can override your personal boundaries, another person’s consent, or platform rules. You can decline or stop work when a request changes into something you cannot accept.
bullets: Set a realistic delivery window and an update point.
State how revisions work and when a change becomes a new request.
Define boundaries before payment, not only after a dispute begins.
Keep the option to decline or pause when scope changes.

sections.heading: Use a simple request-and-delivery record
paragraphs: Keep the essentials in one organized record: the request, the final scope agreed, the payment confirmation, any revisions, and the delivery confirmation. Use platform records where available and follow applicable privacy and retention rules. Avoid collecting unnecessary identity or personal details from the buyer. A concise record can help you answer a later question without retaining more sensitive information than the work requires.

After delivery, send a neutral confirmation that identifies what was delivered and where, without adding a new promise. If the platform offers a status or receipt feature, use it according to its instructions. Do not assume that a sent message proves the recipient opened or accepted the work; distinguish what you can document from what you cannot verify.

table.caption: A compact custom-request record
rows: Vague promises such as “anything you want”
Date, permitted delivery location, confirmation sent
Claiming the recipient viewed it unless verified
What changed and the agreed next step
Editing or deleting records needed to resolve a dispute

sections.heading: Plan for cancellations, delays, and changed requests
paragraphs: Set expectations for a request that cannot be completed as planned. Review the platform’s current refund, cancellation, and dispute procedures rather than inventing a private policy that conflicts with them. Explain how you will communicate a delay and what choices are available, where platform rules allow choices. Do not promise a refund outcome that you do not control.

When a request changes materially, stop and summarize the change in writing. Confirm whether the revised scope is allowed and whether the platform provides a permitted way to adjust the transaction. If it does not, do not improvise a workaround. Preserve relevant records and use the platform’s support or dispute route when needed. A calm, factual explanation is more useful than arguing about motives.
bullets: Check cancellation and dispute procedures before accepting requests.
Send a brief update if the delivery window becomes uncertain.
Get written agreement to any permitted scope change.
Keep communications factual and within the platform’s rules.

sections.heading: Make the workflow sustainable
paragraphs: Custom work can become difficult to manage when each request is negotiated from scratch. Use a reusable intake form or message template that asks only for information needed to assess the request. Include a clear decline option and do not invite sensitive information that is not necessary. Track workload so the number of accepted requests does not exceed the time you can reasonably devote to them.

Review the template after policy changes, recurring misunderstandings, or a request that exposed a gap in your process. Remove language that readers interpret differently than intended. A good workflow does not guarantee agreement or eliminate disputes; it makes the offer, boundaries, and records clearer before expectations diverge.
bullets: Limit intake to details necessary to evaluate the request.
Use consistent language for scope, timing, and revisions.
Decline work that does not fit your capacity or boundaries.
Update templates when policy or recurring questions reveal a gap.

faqs.question: Should I accept payment before the scope is clear?
faqs.answer: It is safer to clarify the deliverable, limits, timing, and permitted transaction route first. If the platform’s process requires payment at a particular point, make sure the terms are still clear before proceeding with the work.

faqs.question: Can I move a custom request to a different payment service?
faqs.answer: Do not assume that off-platform payment is permitted. Check the platform’s current rules and use only an allowed transaction path. A different route may affect platform protections or violate its terms.

faqs.question: What if the buyer asks for something outside the original agreement?
faqs.answer: Pause and restate the agreed scope and the requested change. Check whether the revised request is allowed, then agree on a permitted next step or decline. Do not treat the original payment as consent to unlimited changes.

faqs.question: How much information should I keep after delivery?
faqs.answer: Keep only records needed for ordinary business administration, policy compliance, or resolving a potential issue, and follow applicable rules. Avoid retaining unnecessary sensitive details or payment credentials.
